planting.note: Direct sow in hills or rows after soil has warmed following last frost; in Gulf Coast gardens a second sowing in midsummer keeps production going once early plants decline from squash vine borer or powdery mildew.

directions: Fordhook Zucchini was bred at Burpee's historic Fordhook Farm trial grounds in Pennsylvania and became an early All-America Selections winner, predating most of the modern hybrid zucchini lines still sold today. It forms a compact, upright bush rather than a sprawling vine, producing straight to slightly curved, smooth dark-green fruit best picked young at 6-8 inches for the most tender, seedless texture. Because it sets fruit heavily and quickly, plants benefit from daily harvesting during peak summer heat to prevent oversized, seedy squash and to keep new blossoms coming. Its open-pollinated seed can be saved true from year to year, unlike the many F1 hybrids that have largely replaced it in seed catalogs.

planting.note: Direct sow in hills 2-3 weeks after last frost once soil is reliably warm; thin to two or three vigorous seedlings per hill and give plenty of room to ramble.

directions: Golden Gopher was released by the University of Minnesota in the 1930s from a cross thought to include honeydew parentage, giving it unusually high sugar content and useful resistance to fusarium wilt for a melon of its era, though it remains susceptible to powdery mildew. The lightly ribbed, sparsely netted, roughly two-and-a-half-pound fruits carry deep orange flesh of excellent eating quality and are known among growers as 'pop open' melons for how they sometimes split at the blossom end when fully ripe. Its compact vine and dependable production have kept it in circulation with small seed stewardship organizations long after most other university-bred melons of its generation disappeared from commerce. Watch fruit closely as it nears maturity and harvest promptly once it slips or begins to crack to avoid loss to splitting.

planting.note: Direct sow after danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed; trellising keeps the long fruit straighter and reduces contact with humid, disease-prone soil in Southern gardens.

directions: Dating to at least 1842, Long Green Improved was for decades the standard American slicing and pickling cucumber before modern hybrids took over seed racks, and it remains one of the longest-cultivated open-pollinated cucumbers still commercially available. Vigorous vines produce dark green, often faintly ribbed fruit that can be picked small for pickles or left to grow 8-10 inches or more for fresh slicing, with crisp, mild flesh that holds up well in hot weather. Because it is an old-style monoecious variety rather than a modern gynoecious hybrid, it needs both male and female flowers present for pollination, so plant a full row rather than just one or two hills to ensure good fruit set. Save seed from fully ripened (yellowed) fruit for a true-breeding crop next season.

planting.note: Direct sow once soil has warmed after last frost; its early maturity makes it a good choice for a spring crop ahead of Gulf Coast summer heat and disease pressure, plus a possible fall sowing.

directions: Early Fortune was selected by a Michigan grower from the older Davis Perfect cucumber and introduced commercially around 1910 as an early, dependable white-spine slicer, quickly becoming one of the most widely planted cucumbers in the country. Fruits reach 7-8 inches with smooth, deep green skin and crisp, mild white flesh, and the vines begin bearing notably faster than many other open-pollinated slicers of similar type. It is a traditional monoecious variety needing insect pollination between separate male and female blossoms, so plant in blocks rather than single rows for reliable fruit set. Its short time to harvest and long production history make it a forgiving choice for gardeners wanting a classic slicing cucumber without relying on modern hybrid seed.

planting.note: Direct sow in warm soil after last frost; its compact bush habit suits raised beds and smaller Gulf Coast garden plots better than sprawling vine-type squash.

directions: Nero di Milano, meaning 'black of Milan,' is a traditional Italian zucchini from Lombardy prized in home gardens for its very dark, near-black-green skin and compact, open bush growth habit that makes fruit easy to spot and pick. It is among the earliest zucchini to begin bearing, and fruit is best harvested young at 6-8 inches, when the skin is tender and the flavor sweetest. The tidy, non-sprawling plant produces steadily over a long season, making it a practical choice for gardeners who want continuous zucchini without the vine sprawl of many other summer squash types. As an open-pollinated Italian heirloom, its seed can be saved true from year to year.

planting.note: Direct sow in warm soil once frost danger has passed; needs a long, warm growing season, so in short-season areas start indoors 3 weeks early, though Gulf Coast gardeners can generally direct sow with time to spare.

directions: Zeppelin is a modern open-pollinated delicata bred by organic seed growers to improve on older delicata strains, selected specifically for better disease tolerance and more uniform, elongated cream-and-green striped fruit. Like other delicata types the thin, edible skin means the whole squash can be roasted without peeling, and the dense, sweet, corn-and-chestnut-like flesh has made delicata squash increasingly popular at farmers markets. Vines run further than bush delicata types, so give them room to sprawl or train them up a sturdy trellis to save garden space. Because it is a stable open-pollinated variety rather than a hybrid, seed can be saved from isolated plantings for a true-breeding crop.

planting.note: Direct sow in hills after soil has warmed well past last frost; bred from Florida stock, it is naturally well suited to the long, humid growing season of Gulf Coast gardens.

directions: Strawberry Watermelon was selected from an older Florida heirloom by grower Walt Childs and introduced by Southern Exposure Seed Exchange in 1989, making it a relatively recent release built on genetics already adapted to hot, humid Southern conditions. The long, dark green striped fruits reach 15-25 pounds when well fed and watered, with vivid strawberry-red flesh, white seeds, and very good disease resistance for an heirloom watermelon. It shows good tolerance of common Southern disease pressure compared to many older watermelon heirlooms, making it a practical choice for humid Gulf Coast summers. Give vines ample room to run and consistent moisture while fruit is sizing for the best flavor and texture.

planting.note: Direct sow in hills after last frost once soil is warm; its tolerance of humidity and uneven rainfall makes it a solid pick for muggy Gulf Coast summers where many melons struggle with fruit splitting.

directions: Kansas Muskmelon is a Great Plains heirloom kept alive through regional seed savers and now offered by Southern Exposure Seed Exchange, valued for holding up to humid weather and inconsistent rainfall better than many other old melon varieties. The oval, sutured, moderately netted fruits average about four pounds and ripen almost all the way out to the rind for little waste, with fine-textured, richly flavored flesh that has kept the variety in demand among heirloom growers. It also shows good resistance to sap beetles, a common pest that ruins fruit of other melon varieties late in the season. As with other open-pollinated melons, isolate plantings from other Cucumis melo varieties if you intend to save true seed.
